newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - Lamfalussy praises Britain on BOE move.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Lamfalussy praises Britain on BOE move.

text.p: Alexandre Lamfalussy, president of the European Monetary Institute, on Tuesday praised Britain's move to give the Bank of England operational leeway and called for greater central bank independence across the EU.

Britain's decision, announced last week by the new Labour government, brought the country a significant step nearer Europe's monetary union criteria, Lamfalussy said in a speech to a conference organised by the Austrian National Bank.

"This is music to my ears. It is a very important decision. It goes quite a way towards meeting the requirements of the Maastricht Treaty," said Lamfalussy, who heads the forerunner to the European Central Bank.
Asked by reporters how he rated Britain's chances of being among the first group of nations to introduce a single currency, he replied: "It is less unlikely."
"I would be delighted to have Britain as part of the first group of (countries in) European Economic and Monetary Union," he continued.
In his speech, Lamfalussy called for greater central bank independence throughout the 15-member EU in preparation for the planned introduction of a single currency in January 1999.
"That has to be done now. There are very few countries which have completely done the job," he said, without elaborating.
The European Monetary Institute president expressed confidence that the future European Central Bank would manage to pursue an independent policy geared towards price stability under monetary union.
Already EU central banks had succeeded in cutting the bloc's average annual inflation to little over two percent, he noted.

"If this has become possible in Stage Two (of European Economic and Monetary Union)...why should it change when the central banks act jointly within the framework of the European System of Central Banks (ESBC)?" Lamfalussy asked.

The independence of the European Central Bank, as defined in the Maastricht Treaty, was necessary to underpin the credibility of monetary policy and was a key condition for the maintenance of price stability, he argued.
"The door to the single monetary policy is locked from both sides, and neither the ESCB nor third parties can open the door for political instructions," Lamfalussy said.

While the ECOFIN Council of EU finance ministers would be able to agree formal exchange rate arrangements with non-EU countries, Lamfalussy ruled out that this would interfere with the workings of the European Central Bank.
"To begin with, the participation of the euro in a multinational system with non-EU currencies is, to say the least, not on the agenda," Lamfalussy said.
